title: MF Distributor
blurb: Mutual fund distribution: suitability, discipline and service across the life of an investment.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays, niche topics)
One 60–75 minute session, plus 15 minutes of role-play and the quiz
None for awareness; NISM Series V-A and an EUIN before dealing with clients
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway
outcomes: Explain the MF ecosystem and the distributor's role and limits in plain words.
Run a discovery and risk-profiling conversation before suggesting any fund.
Onboard a client correctly, with every disclosure made.
Conduct an annual review that goes beyond "your SIP is running".
Keep a client invested through a market fall without making promises.

sources: SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds (current edition)
SEBI circular on categorisation and rationalisation of mutual fund schemes (Oct 2017) and later amendments
SEBI circulars on the riskometer and Potential Risk Class (2020 and 2021)
SEBI circular on uniform cut-off timings and NAV applicability
SEBI: investor grievance redress via SCORES and Smart ODR (2023 onwards)
AMFI Code of Conduct and distributor guidelines; NISM Series V-A: Mutual Fund Distributors certification workbook
Income-tax Act and Finance Act provisions on capital gains from mutual funds (verify current rates each year)

cards.q: Why is keeping a client invested the distributor's real job?
a: ₹10,000/month SIP at an assumed 12% a year:
10 yrs: ₹12 L invested → about ₹23 L
20 yrs: ₹24 L → about ₹1 Cr
The last 10 years alone add about ₹2.5 Cr, so stopping early costs the most. (Illustration only, not a promise.)

cards.q: What does L.E.A.R.N. stand for?
a: L: Learn the basics
E: Evaluate the client
A: Act right
R: Review & rebalance
N: Navigate behaviour

cards.q: Who regulates mutual funds and MF intermediaries in India?
a: SEBI. It sets the rules on categories, costs, disclosures and investor protection.

cards.q: What do the Sponsor and Trustees do?
a: The sponsor sets up the fund; the trustees protect unitholders' interests. They are an independent layer watching the fund house.

cards.q: What is the AMC's role?
a: The AMC (fund house) manages the money as per each scheme's mandate. The fund manager decides what to buy within the scheme's rules.

cards.q: Who holds a mutual fund scheme's securities?
a: The custodian. Investor money is not held by the AMC or by the distributor.

cards.q: What is an RTA? Name the two main RTAs.
a: Registrar & Transfer Agent: CAMS and KFintech. Maintains investor records, processes transactions, issues statements, and handles folios, nominations and service requests.

cards.q: What does AMFI do?
a: Industry body that registers distributors (ARN), runs investor awareness and sets the distributor code of conduct.

cards.q: What is an ARN?
a: AMFI Registration Number: the distributor's registration with AMFI, renewed periodically.

cards.q: What is an EUIN, and who needs one?
a: Employee Unique Identification Number. Every person who deals with clients needs NISM Series V-A certification and an EUIN, quoted on every transaction they handle.

cards.q: Distributor vs SEBI RIA: what can't a distributor do?
a: Cannot charge an advisory fee or call themselves an "independent adviser". Describe yourself as a "Mutual Fund Distributor"; guidance must be incidental to selling products.

cards.q: Direct plan vs regular plan?
a: Direct: bought straight from the AMC. Regular: bought through a distributor. It has a higher expense ratio because the AMC pays the distributor's trail commission from the TER.

cards.q: How does a distributor earn, and how is it disclosed?
a: Trail commission from the AMC, paid only while the client stays invested. No upfront commission is allowed. The commission and expense ratio are shown in the client's CAS.

cards.q: What is the foundation check before investing?
a: Emergency fund in place (several months of expenses)
Adequate term life and health insurance
High-interest debt (credit cards, personal loans) being cleared
If missing, fix these first.

cards.q: Define risk capacity.
a: How much loss the client can AFFORD, judged by age, income stability, dependants, existing assets and horizon.

cards.q: Define risk tolerance.
a: How much loss the client can STOMACH, judged by past reactions to market falls, comfort questions and a questionnaire.

cards.q: Define risk need.
a: How much risk the goal actually REQUIRES: goal amount vs current savings and time left.

cards.q: Golden rule of risk profiling?
a: Match recommendations to the LOWER of capacity and tolerance. Re-profile after major life events. (A wealthy client who panics in falls is still a moderate investor.)

cards.q: What 4 things do you capture for every goal?
a: What the goal is
Amount in today's money
Target year
Priority: must-have or nice-to-have

cards.q: The 5 discovery questions?
a: What is this money for, and when will you need it?
Have you invested before? What happened in the last market fall?
If this fell 20% next year, what would you do?
Who else in the family is involved in money decisions?
What do you already hold (EPF, PPF, FDs, property)?

cards.q: Categories for a goal under 1 year / emergency money?
a: Liquid, overnight, money market funds, for stability and quick access.

cards.q: Categories for a 1–3 year goal?
a: Short-duration debt, arbitrage, conservative hybrid, to limit equity swings.

cards.q: Categories for a 3–5 year goal?
a: Balanced advantage, hybrid, some large-cap, for moderate growth with cushioning.

cards.q: Categories for a 7+ year goal?
a: Flexi-cap, large & mid-cap, index funds, mid/small-cap within limits. There is time to ride out equity cycles.

cards.q: What is ELSS, and what is its key feature?
a: Tax-saving equity fund with a 3-year lock-in for each SIP instalment, counted from that instalment's own date. Suits long-term savers.

cards.q: SIP vs lump sum?
a: SIP: regular amounts from income; averages purchase cost over time. Lump sum: for long horizons when the money is available now.

cards.q: What is an STP and when do you use it?
a: Systematic Transfer Plan: park a large sum in a debt or liquid fund and transfer it into equity over 6–12 months, reducing timing regret.

cards.q: What is an SWP?
a: Systematic Withdrawal Plan: regular withdrawals later, e.g. in retirement.

cards.q: The onboarding checklist?
a: KYC verified (not on hold) · FATCA/CRS done
Holding mode chosen deliberately
Nomination registered, or opt-out recorded
Bank mandate for SIPs
Riskometer shown and matched to profile
Exit load, lock-in, expense ratio explained
Commission and direct-plan option disclosed
Recommendation and reason recorded

cards.q: How often should a client be reviewed, and what is the agenda?
a: At least once a year (30–45 min):
Life update · Goal progress · Performance
Allocation check · Overlap & clutter
Step-up · Housekeeping
Written next-actions summary

cards.q: Which return measure suits SIPs?
a: XIRR. It accounts for each instalment's date. Mistake: using simple or absolute return for SIPs.

cards.q: When is CAGR the right measure?
a: For a single lump-sum investment. Mistake: applying it to SIPs.

cards.q: When is absolute return meaningful?
a: Only over very short periods. Mistake: judging a 5-year holding by total % gain.

cards.q: How do you judge a fund manager?
a: Against the fund's benchmark and category average over 3 and 5 years, never on one good or bad year.

cards.q: 4 valid reasons to recommend switching a fund?
a: Consistent underperformance vs benchmark & peers over 3+ years
Change in fund manager or investment style
Change in the scheme's mandate or category
Change in the client's goal or horizon

cards.q: What must you check before ANY switch?
a: Exit load and tax.

cards.q: What does a 10% yearly SIP step-up do?
a: ₹10,000/month, assumed 12%, 20 years: flat SIP ≈ ₹1 Cr (₹24 L invested); 10% step-up ≈ ₹1.99 Cr (₹68.7 L invested). Illustration only.

cards.q: The 6-step market-fall playbook?
a: Call first, before clients call in panic
Reconnect to the goal, not the day's loss
Explain the SIP advantage (more units)
Use history, without promises
Act only if the plan says so
Record the conversation; follow up in writing

cards.q: In a fall, which clients do you call first?
a: Recent and first-time investors.

cards.q: "Let me stop my SIP until markets settle." Bias and response?
a: Loss aversion. "Your SIP is buying more units at lower prices now. Stopping skips the part that helps most later."

cards.q: "My friend's fund gave 40%. Let's switch." Bias and response?
a: Recency / herd. "Let's compare both over 5 years and see how each did in bad years."

cards.q: "I'll sell when it's back to my cost." Bias and response?
a: Anchoring. "Your buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next. Is it still the right fund for your goal?"

cards.q: Why does a falling NAV help a SIP investor?
a: The same instalment buys more units. In the training example the average cost (₹85.6) came in below the average NAV (₹87.3), and ₹1.2 L invested grew to ≈ ₹1.51 L.

cards.q: What happened in March 2020?
a: The Nifty 50 fell close to 40% in about a month (closed 7,610 on 23 Mar). By Feb 2021 it had nearly doubled from that low. Those who stopped or redeemed at the bottom locked in losses.

cards.q: The investor emotion cycle: when do most investors buy and sell?
a: Most buy at euphoria (the top, when risk is highest) and sell at despondency (the bottom, just before recovery). Our job is to move clients against their emotions.

cards.q: What must retention NEVER become?
a: Switching or churning for commission
Pushing NFOs or new categories without a clear fit
Assuring returns, capital protection or recovery timelines

cards.q: Transmission after death: what speeds it up?
a: A registered nominee. Without one, legal heirs must prove their claim. The claimant also needs KYC. Every folio needs a nominee.

cards.q: What happens to a minor's folio at 18?
a: It needs KYC and a status change to major, or transactions get blocked.

cards.q: Is a switch within the same fund house taxable?
a: It can be. A switch is a redemption plus a purchase, so it can trigger tax and exit load.

cards.q: Exit load / ELSS lock-in on a SIP: when are all units free?
a: Each SIP instalment has its own holding period. Exit load applies per unit, redeemed first-in, first-out (FIFO). The LAST instalment decides when all units are free.

cards.q: Client short on cash: cancel the SIP?
a: Ask about a SIP PAUSE. Many fund houses allow a temporary pause instead of cancelling and restarting.

cards.q: How is an SWP taxed?
a: Each withdrawal is part principal and part gain. Only the gain portion is taxed.

cards.q: Is a ₹10 NFO cheaper than a fund at ₹200 NAV?
a: No. New is not cheaper; it is untested. The scheme has no track record.

cards.q: What happens on a change in fundamental attributes?
a: When a scheme's mandate changes, investors get an exit window without exit load.

cards.q: What is a segregated portfolio?
a: In a credit event, a debt fund separates the bad paper. Investors hold units of both until recovery.

cards.q: NRI / FATCA points to check?
a: Some fund houses restrict US/Canada residents. NRE vs NRO account type matters. Confirm eligibility first.

cards.q: What is the CAS?
a: Consolidated Account Statement: one statement showing all folios across fund houses, including commission paid. Sent monthly if there were transactions, otherwise half-yearly. Download it twice a year.

cards.q: Which small costs can change after investing?
a: Stamp duty applies on purchases. Expense ratios can change with notice and with fund size. Check them at each review.

cards.q: What must you quote on every transaction and communication?
a: Your ARN and EUIN.

cards.q: What must accompany any past-performance figure?
a: The standard mutual fund risk disclaimer. Never promise or imply guaranteed returns or recovery timelines.

cards.q: What is the complaint escalation path you share with clients?
a: AMC → SEBI SCORES → Smart ODR. Escalate promptly and never discourage a client from complaining.

cards.q: Key compliance don'ts?
a: Deal with clients before NISM V-A + EUIN
Call yourself an adviser or charge a fee
Sell above the client's risk level
Hide costs or churn for commission
Accept cash or handle client money

cards.q: What is NAV, and how is it calculated?
a: Value of one unit: (investments + cash and receivables, less liabilities) ÷ units outstanding. Calculated every business day.

cards.q: Open-ended vs closed-ended vs interval funds?
a: Open-ended: buy and sell any business day at NAV. Closed-ended: NFO, then the exchange, until maturity. Interval: open only at set intervals.

cards.q: Does a low NAV mean a cheap fund?
a: No. NAV is the price of one unit. Returns depend on the portfolio, not on the unit price.

cards.q: How many riskometer levels are there?
a: Six: Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High. Match the level to the client's profile.

cards.q: What do large, mid and small cap mean?
a: Large cap: top 100 companies. Mid cap: ranked 101 to 250. Small cap: ranked 251 onwards.

cards.q: Can a scheme's riskometer change?
a: Yes. It follows the portfolio, so check it at every review.

cards.q: What is the usual cut-off for most schemes?
a: 3:00 pm on a business day, with funds available. After that, the next business day's NAV applies.

cards.q: Is a switch one transaction?
a: No. A switch is a redemption plus a purchase, each with its own cut-off and NAV.

cards.q: SID, SAI and KIM: what is each?
a: SID: scheme details and risks. SAI: sponsor, trustees and AMC details. KIM: short summary given with the application.

cards.q: What should you point out before a client invests?
a: Objective and category, riskometer, exit load, lock-in and TER, the benchmark, and where to find the SID and factsheet.

cards.q: How are equity fund gains broadly taxed?
a: Short term (up to 12 months) and long term (over 12 months) are taxed at different rates, with a yearly exemption on long-term gains. Check current rates.

cards.q: How are specified debt fund gains taxed?
a: For funds bought on or after 1 April 2023, gains are taxed at the client's slab rate regardless of holding period. Check current rules.

cards.q: Who gives personal tax advice?
a: A tax adviser or CA. A distributor explains the basics only.

cards.q: What does the TER pay for?
a: Running the scheme, including the fund manager, administration and, in a regular plan, the distributor's trail commission.

cards.q: Index fund vs ETF?
a: Index fund: bought from the AMC at NAV. ETF: traded on the exchange at market price through a demat account.

cards.q: What is a fund of funds?
a: A fund that invests in other funds' units. Costs sit at two levels and tax follows the underlying fund type.

cards.q: MF vs PMS vs AIF minimum ticket?
a: MF: a few hundred rupees. PMS: ₹50 lakh. AIF: typically ₹1 crore.

questions.q: Who holds the securities of a mutual fund scheme?
questions.why: An independent custodian holds the fund's securities. Investor money is never held by the AMC or the distributor.

questions.q: Which body registers mutual fund distributors and issues the ARN?
questions.why: AMFI is the industry body that registers distributors (ARN). SEBI is the regulator.

questions.q: Who needs an EUIN?
o: Only the head of the distribution firm
Only employees handling lump sums above ₹1 lakh
Every employee who deals with clients
questions.why: Each person dealing with clients needs NISM Series V-A and an EUIN, quoted on every transaction they handle.

questions.q: Why is a regular plan's expense ratio higher than a direct plan's?
o: It includes the distributor's trail commission
It pays a higher fund-manager salary
It includes stamp duty on every purchase
questions.why: The regular plan carries the trail commission, which the AMC pays from the TER, only while the client stays invested. It is shown in the CAS.

questions.q: A distributor wants to charge a client ₹5,000 for a financial plan. What is correct?
o: Not allowed; charging for advice requires SEBI RIA registration
Allowed once a year at the annual review
questions.why: Distributors give guidance incidental to selling and cannot charge an advisory fee or call themselves independent advisers.

questions.q: Before suggesting any fund, what must be checked first?
o: Emergency fund, term and health insurance, and high-interest debt
questions.why: The foundation check comes first. If it is missing, fixing it is the first recommendation.

questions.q: A wealthy client with high risk capacity panics and sells in every market fall. How should they be profiled?
o: Moderate: match to the lower of capacity and tolerance
Aggressive, to make up for past losses
questions.why: Recommendations follow the LOWER of capacity and tolerance. Low tolerance sets the limit.

questions.q: "How much risk the goal actually requires" describes:
questions.why: Risk need compares the goal amount with current savings and time left.

questions.q: Which discovery question reveals the most about risk tolerance?
o: "How many bank accounts do you have?"
"What happened during the last market fall?"
questions.why: Past behaviour in a fall says more about tolerance than any questionnaire.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four things captured for every goal?
o: The fund the client has already chosen
questions.why: For every goal capture: what it is, amount in today's money, target year and priority.

questions.q: A client needs money in 8 months. Which categories fit?
o: Liquid, overnight or money market funds
questions.why: Under 1 year / emergency money needs stability and quick access.

questions.q: A client has a 2-year goal. Which categories should be considered?
questions.why: 1–3 year goals should have limited exposure to equity swings.

questions.q: A client has ₹20 lakh for a 10-year goal but fears investing at the wrong time. Best method?
o: STP from a liquid/debt fund into equity over 6–12 months
Invest all of it in small-cap today
Keep it in a savings account until markets fall
questions.why: STP stages a large sum into equity and reduces timing regret.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of the onboarding checklist?
o: Riskometer matched to the client's profile
questions.why: Returns are never guaranteed. Promising them is a compliance breach.

questions.q: An SWP is best suited for:
o: Building a corpus from monthly income
Moving money between two equity funds
questions.why: SWP provides regular withdrawals; SIP is for accumulation from income.

questions.q: How often should a client receive a structured review, at minimum?
questions.why: A yearly structured review is where most long-term value is added.

questions.q: Which return measure should be used for a SIP portfolio?
questions.why: XIRR accounts for each instalment's date. CAGR is for a single lump sum.

questions.q: Which is a valid reason to recommend switching out of a fund?
o: Underperformance vs benchmark and peers over 3+ years
A friend's fund returned 40% last year
questions.why: Other valid reasons are a manager/style change, a mandate change, or a change in the client's goal.

questions.q: ₹10,000/month at an assumed 12% for 20 years, stepped up 10% every year, ends at about:
questions.why: A flat SIP ends at ≈₹1 Cr. The 10% step-up nearly doubles it to ≈₹1.99 Cr (illustration only).

questions.q: Before recommending any switch, the distributor must always check:
o: The NAV of the new fund
Whether the new fund is an NFO
questions.why: A switch is a redemption plus a purchase, so it can trigger exit load and tax.

questions.q: Markets fall 15%. What is the first thing you do?
o: Wait for clients to call you
Advise all clients to pause SIPs
Proactively call clients, starting with recent and first-time investors
Move all equity holdings to debt
questions.why: Call first, before clients call in panic, and reconnect them to their goals.

questions.q: "I'll sell when it's back to my cost." Which bias is this?
questions.why: The buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next. Ask if it's still the right fund for the goal.

questions.q: "My friend's fund gave 40%. Let's switch." Which bias is this?
questions.why: Respond by comparing both funds over 5 years, including how each did in bad years.

questions.q: When the NAV falls, what happens to a running SIP?
o: The same instalment buys more units
questions.why: Lower prices mean more units, which lowers the average cost per unit.

questions.q: Which statement is acceptable to a client during a market fall?
o: "Let's move into this new NFO instead."
"Falls like this have happened before; let's look at your goal and horizon."
questions.why: Use history without promises. Never assure returns, capital protection or recovery timelines.

questions.q: A client switches from Fund A to Fund B in the same fund house. Can it be taxable?
o: Yes, because a switch is a redemption plus a purchase
No, switches within one fund house are tax-free
Only if the amount exceeds ₹1 lakh
Only exit load applies, never tax
questions.why: Check tax and exit load before every switch, even within the same fund house.

questions.q: A client started an ELSS SIP 3 years ago. Are all units free of lock-in?
o: Yes, lock-in counts from the first instalment
No, each instalment has its own 3-year lock-in
No, ELSS units are locked for 5 years
questions.why: Each SIP instalment unlocks 3 years after its own date, so the last instalment decides when all units are free.

questions.q: A minor's folio when the child turns 18:
o: Needs KYC and a status change, or transactions get blocked
questions.why: Remind families to update a child's folio at 18.

questions.q: A new NFO is offered at ₹10 NAV. What is true?
o: It is not cheaper; it is untested and has no track record
It is cheaper than a fund with a ₹200 NAV
It is guaranteed to grow faster
It carries lower risk than existing funds
questions.why: NAV level says nothing about value. New is not cheaper, only untested.

questions.q: Which escalation path should clients be told about?
o: AMC, then SEBI SCORES, then Smart ODR
questions.why: Escalate complaints promptly and never discourage a client from complaining.
